lead: A laminate is a stack of plies bonded together, each at its own fibre angle. Every ply is rotated to the laminate axes and then added up through the thickness, which gives three stiffness matrices: A for stretching, D for bending and B for the coupling between them. These turn the mid-plane strains and curvatures of a panel into forces and moments per unit width. They are how wing skins, spars and blades are given the stiffness they need, and how a composite strip is given its beam stiffness EI.
prereq: You need: the rotated ply stiffness Q̄ from composites: FRP and orthotropic plies, and the curvatures of pure bending of thin plates.

sections.h3: From plies to A, B and D

blocks.text: Describe a laminate by its stacking sequence, the ply angles from one face to the other, such as [0/90/90/0], written [0/90]<sub>s</sub> because it is symmetric about the mid-plane. Measure z from the mid-plane; ply k lies between z<sub>k</sub>−1 and z<sub>k</sub>.

Classical laminate theory makes the Kirchhoff assumption for the whole stack: the strain at height z is the mid-plane strain plus z times the curvature, ε = ε⁰ + zκ. Each ply turns its strain into stress through its own Q̄. Integrating stress through the thickness gives the force per unit width N; integrating stress times z gives the moment per unit width M. Because Q̄ is constant within a ply, the integrals become sums:

A<sub>ij</sub> = Σ Q̄<sub>ij,k</sub> (z<sub>k</sub> − z<sub>k</sub>−1),   B<sub>ij</sub> = ½ Σ Q̄<sub>ij,k</sub> (z<sub>k</sub>² − z<sub>k</sub>−1²),   D<sub>ij</sub> = ⅓ Σ Q̄<sub>ij,k</sub> (z<sub>k</sub>³ − z<sub>k</sub>−1³)
blocks.where: A<sub>ij</sub> is the extensional stiffness (N/mm); B<sub>ij</sub> the coupling stiffness (N); D<sub>ij</sub> the bending stiffness (N·mm); Q̄ in N/mm² (1 GPa = 1000 N/mm²); z in mm; i, j = 1, 2, 6.

blocks.text: A weights every ply by its thickness, so it does not depend on the order of the plies. D weights each ply by roughly z² times its thickness, so the outer plies dominate bending. B weights plies by z, with opposite signs above and below the mid-plane.

blocks.where: N = (N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub>, N<sub>xy</sub>) are the in-plane forces per unit width (N/mm); M = (M<sub>x</sub>, M<sub>y</sub>, M<sub>xy</sub>) the moments per unit width (N·mm/mm); ε⁰ the mid-plane strains; κ the curvatures (mm⁻¹).

blocks.text: In a symmetric laminate every ply at +z has a twin at −z, their contributions to B cancel, and B = 0: N = Aε⁰ and M = Dκ, so stretching and bending are independent. In an unsymmetric laminate B ≠ 0: an in-plane load bends the plate and a moment stretches it. The same coupling makes an unsymmetric laminate warp as it cools after cure, because the thermal contraction of the plies acts as an in-plane load.

A balanced laminate has a −θ ply for every +θ ply, which makes A<sub>16</sub> = A<sub>26</sub> = 0 so that in-plane loads cause no shear. D<sub>16</sub> and D<sub>26</sub> still survive unless the twins are mirrored about the mid-plane; they couple bending and twisting, which designers use on purpose in aeroelastic tailoring.

A laminate strip of width b bent about an axis across it behaves as a beam only if we say what happens across the width. If the strip is held so that κ<sub>y</sub> = 0, as in cylindrical bending, M<sub>x</sub> = D<sub>11</sub>κ<sub>x</sub> and EI = bD<sub>11</sub>.

A narrow beam is free to curl sideways, so M<sub>y</sub> = 0 instead. For a symmetric laminate with no bend–twist coupling, M<sub>y</sub> = D<sub>12</sub>κ<sub>x</sub> + D<sub>22</sub>κ<sub>y</sub> = 0 gives κ<sub>y</sub> = −(D<sub>12</sub>/D<sub>22</sub>)κ<sub>x</sub>, and then:

blocks.where: EI is the bending stiffness of a narrow symmetric laminate beam (N·mm²); b its width (mm); D<sub>11</sub>, D<sub>12</sub>, D<sub>22</sub> the bending stiffnesses per unit width (N·mm).

blocks.text: This is the laminate form of the anticlastic case for an isotropic plate, where the same algebra gives D(1 − ν²) = Et³/12. A wide panel is closer to κ<sub>y</sub> = 0; real beams lie between the two limits.

figure.caption: The worked [0/90]<sub>s</sub> laminate. The two outer 0° plies sit between z = ±0.125 and ±0.25 mm and give 1284.3 of the 1297.4 N·mm of D<sub>11</sub> (99%), against 93% of A<sub>11</sub>: bending stiffness is set by the outer plies, because D weights each ply by z².

A note says the outer plies give 99 percent of D 1 1 but only 93 percent of A 1 1.

examples.question: A [0/90]<sub>s</sub> laminate has four carbon/epoxy plies, each 0.125 mm thick, with Q<sub>11</sub> = 140.91 GPa, Q<sub>22</sub> = 10.06 GPa, Q<sub>12</sub> = 3.02 GPa and Q<sub>66</sub> = 5.00 GPa. Find A<sub>11</sub>, D<sub>11</sub>, D<sub>12</sub> and D<sub>22</sub>, the value of B, and the bending stiffness of a 100 mm wide strip held flat across and free to curl.
steps: Total thickness 0.5 mm. Interfaces from the mid-plane: z = −0.25, −0.125, 0, 0.125, 0.25 mm. Plies: 0° outside, 90° inside. For a 90° ply Q̄<sub>11</sub> = Q<sub>22</sub> and Q̄<sub>22</sub> = Q<sub>11</sub>; Q̄<sub>12</sub> = Q<sub>12</sub> for both.
Cube differences: an outer ply has 0.25³ − 0.125³ = 0.013672 mm³, an inner ply 0.125³ − 0 = 0.001953 mm³ (two of each).
B = 0: each ply at +z has an identical ply at −z, and their (z<sub>k</sub>² − z<sub>k</sub>−1²) terms are equal and opposite.
Held flat across: EI = bD<sub>11</sub> = 100 × 1297.4 = 129,740 N·mm².
Free to curl: EI = 100 × (1297.4 − 31.45²/275.2) = 100 × (1297.4 − 3.59) = 129,381 N·mm², 0.28% less. D<sub>12</sub> is small for a cross-ply, so the two limits are close.
examples.answer: A<sub>11</sub> = 37,743 N/mm; D<sub>11</sub> = 1297.4, D<sub>22</sub> = 275.2, D<sub>12</sub> = 31.45 N·mm; B = 0; EI = 129,740 N·mm² held flat and 129,381 N·mm² free.

examples.question: A two-ply [0/90] laminate (0° ply below, 90° ply above, each 0.125 mm, same plies) is pulled by N<sub>x</sub> = 10 N/mm with no moment. Find A<sub>11</sub>, B<sub>11</sub> and D<sub>11</sub>, then solve the full laminate equations for the mid-plane strain and the curvature.
steps: Solving the 6 × 6 system [A B; B D][ε⁰; κ] = [10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] (with A<sub>12</sub> = 754.9, A<sub>22</sub> = 18,871 N/mm and D<sub>12</sub> = 3.932, D<sub>22</sub> = 98.29 N·mm): ε<sub>x</sub>⁰ = 1.22 × 10⁻³, κ<sub>x</sub> = 1.27 × 10⁻² mm⁻¹, and κ<sub>y</sub> is zero to rounding.

The in-plane pull bends the strip to a radius of about 1/|κ<sub>x</sub>| = 79 mm. A laminate with B = 0 would stay flat with ε<sub>x</sub>⁰ close to N<sub>x</sub>/A<sub>11</sub> = 5.30 × 10⁻⁴; with coupling the effective in-plane stiffness A − BD⁻¹B is lower, so the mid-plane strain is more than doubled.
Check of the first row: A<sub>11</sub>ε<sub>x</sub>⁰ + A<sub>12</sub>ε<sub>y</sub>⁰ + B<sub>11</sub>κ<sub>x</sub> + B<sub>12</sub>κ<sub>y</sub> = 10.000 N/mm, the applied 10 N/mm.
examples.answer: A<sub>11</sub> = 18,871 N/mm, B<sub>11</sub> = −1,022 N, D<sub>11</sub> = 98.29 N·mm; ε<sub>x</sub>⁰ = 1.22 × 10⁻³ and κ<sub>x</sub> = 1.27 × 10⁻² mm⁻¹: pulling the unsymmetric laminate bends it.

traps: Using Q instead of Q̄ for a 90° ply. At 90° Q̄<sub>11</sub> = Q<sub>22</sub>, not Q<sub>11</sub>.
Measuring z from the bottom face. All z are from the mid-plane, so the signs of B come out right.
Expecting B = 0 for every laminate. Only a laminate symmetric about its mid-plane has B = 0.
Forgetting the unit change: 1 GPa·mm = 1000 N/mm and 1 GPa·mm³ = 1000 N·mm.
Using EI = bD<sub>11</sub> for a narrow beam free to curl. That holds only for κ<sub>y</sub> = 0 or D<sub>12</sub> = 0; otherwise EI = b(D<sub>11</sub> − D<sub>12</sub>²/D<sub>22</sub>).

quiz.q: Name the matrices A, B and D and give their units.
quiz.a: A extensional stiffness (N/mm), B extension–bending coupling stiffness (N), D bending stiffness (N·mm).

quiz.q: Why is B zero for a symmetric laminate?
quiz.a: Each ply at +z has an identical ply at −z. Their contributions Q̄(z<sub>k</sub>² − z<sub>k</sub>−1²)/2 are equal and opposite, so the sum vanishes.

quiz.q: A [0/90]<sub>s</sub> laminate has four plies 0.2 mm thick with Q<sub>11</sub> = 150 GPa and Q<sub>22</sub> = 10 GPa. Find A<sub>11</sub>.
For the four-ply laminate of the first example, the stacking is changed to [90/0]<sub>s</sub>. Find the new D<sub>11</sub>.
quiz.a: Now the 90° plies are outside: D<sub>11</sub> = ⅓ × 2 × (10.06 × 0.013672 + 140.91 × 0.001953) × 1000 = 275.2 N·mm, against 1297.4 N·mm; A<sub>11</sub> is unchanged.

quiz.q: Why does an unsymmetric laminate warp as it cools after cure, while a symmetric one stays flat?
quiz.a: The plies shrink by different amounts in x and y as they cool, which acts like in-plane loads in each ply. With B ≠ 0 these loads produce curvature, so the panel curls. With B = 0 they only cause in-plane strain and the panel stays flat.

quiz.q: Why does D depend on z³ while A depends only on ply thickness?
quiz.a: The bending strain is zκ, so the stress in a ply is proportional to z, and the moment integrates stress times z: ∫z² dz gives the z³ differences. A integrates stress at uniform strain, ∫dz, giving thickness.

beyond: Not for the exam. Laminate design programs build A, B and D for many plies and pass them to finite element shell elements. Stacking sequences are optimised for stiffness, buckling and strength together, and bend–twist coupling from D<sub>16</sub> is used to reduce gust loads. Search for classical laminate theory and aeroelastic tailoring.
